title: Ethnopharmacological review of medicinal plants used to manage diabetes in Morocco

subsections.subsection_title: Background on Diabetes and the Role of Traditional Medicine
subsections.content:
Diabetes mellitus is a chronic metabolic disorder characterized by persistent hyperglycemia resulting from defects in insulin secretion, insulin action, or both. Its major clinical forms are type 1 diabetes, driven primarily by autoimmune β-cell destruction, and type 2 diabetes, which is dominated by insulin resistance with progressive β-cell dysfunction ref [1], ref [3]. Beyond disturbed glucose homeostasis, diabetes is strongly associated with microvascular and macrovascular complications, including nephropathy, neuropathy, retinopathy, and cardiovascular disease, which account for much of its morbidity and mortality ref [1], ref [3]. The global burden of type 2 diabetes has risen sharply in parallel with population aging, urbanization, sedentary behavior, and nutritional transition, making diabetes a major public-health challenge in both developed and developing settings ref [2], ref [3].

Lifestyle factors are central to this epidemiological transition. Unhealthy dietary patterns, excess caloric intake, obesity, and reduced physical activity increase the risk of insulin resistance and type 2 diabetes, whereas diets rich in fruits, vegetables, whole grains, fiber, fish, magnesium, and unsaturated fats appear protective ref [2]. Nevertheless, for many patients, glycemic control remains difficult to sustain over time, and currently available drugs, although effective, may show limited durability, cost constraints, adverse effects, or inadequate protection against long-term complications ref [1], ref [3]. This therapeutic gap has encouraged sustained interest in complementary strategies, including traditional medicine and plant-based therapies.

Traditional medicine plays a particularly important role in regions where medicinal plants remain culturally embedded, economically accessible, and locally available. Reviews of the antidiabetic literature indicate that hundreds of plant species are used worldwide in folk medicine for diabetes management, although only a fraction have undergone rigorous pharmacological and clinical evaluation ref [1]. Ethnopharmacological research further suggests that many medicinal plants may act through multiple mechanisms relevant to diabetes, such as stimulation of insulin secretion, improvement of insulin sensitivity, inhibition of α-amylase and α-glucosidase, antioxidant effects, modulation of GLUT-4, and attenuation of diabetic complications ref [3]. In this context, documenting Moroccan traditional antidiabetic knowledge is not only of cultural importance, but also a rational starting point for identifying bioactive species with potential value for safer, locally relevant, and mechanistically diverse diabetes management.

subsections.subsection_title: Ethnobotanical and Ethnopharmacological Evidence from Morocco
subsections.content:
Morocco offers particularly rich ethnobotanical evidence for traditional antidiabetic therapy, with surveys from multiple ecological and cultural zones consistently showing extensive reliance on medicinal plants. Early regional studies documented 41 antidiabetic species in oriental Morocco, 54 in Fez–Boulemane, and 92 medicinal plants used for diabetes and related cardiometabolic disorders in Tafilalet, while later work recorded 45 species in Errachidia, 40 in Izarène, 59 in Sidi Slimane, and 76 species in the Central Middle Atlas ref [9], ref [8], ref [10], ref [9], ref [6], ref [4], ref [5]. Together, these surveys indicate both the breadth of Moroccan antidiabetic materia medica and the persistence of phytotherapy across rural and urbanized settings.

Despite regional variation, notable convergences emerge. Lamiaceae, Asteraceae, Apiaceae, and Fabaceae are repeatedly among the most represented families, and a core group of taxa recurs across surveys, including Trigonella foenum-graecum, Olea europaea, Ajuga iva, Artemisia herba-alba, Marrubium vulgare, Rosmarinus officinalis, Nigella sativa, Carum carvi, and Origanum spp. ref [4], ref [5], ref [6], ref [9], ref [8], ref [9]. Leaves and seeds are the plant parts most often employed, decoction and infusion are the dominant preparation methods, and oral administration overwhelmingly predominates ref [4], ref [5], ref [6], ref [9]. These recurrent patterns strengthen the ethnopharmacological signal by suggesting shared empirical selection rather than isolated local practice.

Moroccan surveys also provide important contextual information on use patterns and safety. High proportions of patients reported regular phytotherapy use, frequently because herbal remedies were perceived as cheaper, more effective, or complementary to biomedical treatment; in some regions, medicinal plants were commonly combined with oral antidiabetic drugs or insulin ref [10], ref [8], ref [9]. At the same time, these studies warn that knowledge of toxicity and dosage is often incomplete, and several commonly cited species may present risks at high doses or after prolonged use ref [10], ref [8]. Thus, the Moroccan ethnobotanical record is both a valuable source for candidate antidiabetic plants and a reminder of the need for pharmacological validation and safety standardization ref [8], ref [9].

subsections.subsection_title: Traditional Antidiabetic Knowledge from Other Regions
subsections.content:
Comparative evidence from other regions shows that the traditional management of diabetes is a widespread and structurally coherent body of knowledge rather than an isolated Moroccan phenomenon. In Pakistan, ethnobotanical investigation among traditional health practitioners documented a rich antidiabetic materia medica and emphasized the central role of healers in preserving plant-based therapeutic practices for glycemic control ref [11]. Likewise, a regional review from Central America identified numerous species used not only for diabetes itself but also for its sequelae, highlighting how traditional systems often conceptualize diabetes together with cardiovascular, renal, dermatological, and inflammatory complications ref [12].

A similar pattern is evident in African island and continental settings. In Sudan, 38 plant species from 23 families were reported for diabetes treatment, and notably many of these had already received pharmacological evaluation, while several had progressed to clinical testing for type 2 diabetes ref [13]. In Mauritius, ethnoreligious comparison revealed 52 plant species and multiple polyherbal preparations used against diabetes-related complications, with marked variation in culturally important species across Hindu, Muslim, Christian, and Buddhist communities ref [14]. These studies underscore that traditional antidiabetic knowledge is dynamic, plural, and shaped by local ecology, medical beliefs, and sociocultural identity ref [13], ref [14].

Across these regions, recurrent ethnobotanical themes include frequent use of leaves, decoctions or juices, reliance on polyherbal mixtures, and preference for taxa already familiar as food or household remedies ref [11], ref [12], ref [14]. Such cross-regional convergence is important for Moroccan ethnopharmacological research because it helps distinguish locally specific practices from globally recurring antidiabetic plant-use patterns, thereby strengthening the rationale for comparative prioritization of candidate species for pharmacological validation.

subsections.subsection_title: Preclinical Support for Antidiabetic Medicinal Plants
subsections.content:
Preclinical investigations provide an important pharmacological bridge between ethnobotanical use and antidiabetic plausibility. Experimental studies in chemically induced diabetic rodents consistently show that several traditionally used plants can lower blood glucose, improve dyslipidemia, and modulate pancreatic function. In this context, Peganum harmala seed ethanolic extract produced significant glucose lowering in both sucrose-challenged normoglycemic rats and streptozotocin-induced diabetic rats, with effects at higher doses approaching those of metformin, thereby supporting a genuine antihyperglycemic action rather than a purely folkloric reputation ref [15].

Comparable evidence exists for other medicinal plants widely used in traditional systems. Portulaca oleracea significantly reduced fasting blood glucose, triglycerides, and total cholesterol in alloxan-diabetic rats, while also increasing circulating insulin and suggesting partial protection or restoration of pancreatic beta-cell function; importantly, the study reported no overt toxicity under the tested conditions ref [16]. Petroselinum crispum likewise lowered blood glucose in streptozotocin-diabetic rats, although without clear regeneration of pancreatic B cells, indicating that glycemic improvement may arise through mechanisms other than structural islet repair ref [17]. Together, these models point to multiple possible modes of action, including insulin secretagogue effects, improved peripheral glucose utilization, attenuation of lipid abnormalities, and cytoprotective activity at the pancreatic level ref [15], ref [16], ref [17].

For Moroccan antidiabetic plants, such preclinical findings are especially relevant because many taxa recorded in ethnobotanical surveys are selected on the basis of empirical efficacy but remain insufficiently characterized experimentally. Animal studies therefore help prioritize species for deeper phytochemical and mechanistic work, while also highlighting the need for standardized extracts, dose-response evaluation, subchronic toxicity assessment, and better alignment between traditional preparation modes and laboratory protocols. Overall, the available preclinical literature supports the view that medicinal plants can exert measurable antidiabetic effects, but it also underscores that robust validation requires moving beyond preliminary hypoglycemic screening toward mechanism-oriented and safety-informed investigation ref [15], ref [16], ref [17].

subsections.subsection_title: Regional Ethnobotanical Surveys of Antidiabetic Plant Use
subsections.content:
Regional ethnobotanical surveys in Morocco consistently show that antidiabetic plant use is both widespread and territorially patterned. In the Beni Mellal region, an interview-based survey of 400 informants documented 45 medicinal species from 25 families used in diabetes care, highlighting Olea europaea, Salvia officinalis, Allium sativum, and Trigonella foenum-graecum among the most frequently cited taxa ref [2]. Comparable inventories from other Moroccan settings similarly indicate high species richness but notable regional variation in the dominant plants, reflecting local floristic availability, healer transmission, and sociocultural preferences ref [4], ref [5], ref [6], ref [11], ref [16], ref [17].

Across these surveys, a recurrent core of antidiabetic remedies emerges despite geographic heterogeneity. Frequently reported plants include fenugreek, olive, garlic, Artemisia herba-alba, Ajuga iva, Nigella sativa, and various Lamiaceae and Asteraceae members, usually administered as decoctions, infusions, powders, or macerates ref [2], ref [4], ref [5], ref [6], ref [17]. Surveys from the Central Middle Atlas, Sidi Slimane, Errachidia, Tafilalet, Oriental Morocco, Izarène, and Meknès-Tafilalet collectively suggest that household self-medication coexists with specialist advice from herbalists and traditional healers, with oral preparation of leaves and seeds predominating ref [18], ref [4], ref [5], ref [6], ref [11], ref [16], ref [17].

Taken together, Moroccan regional surveys indicate that ethnobotanical knowledge on diabetes is robust but not uniform. The Beni Mellal study is especially important because it explicitly frames plant use within an integrative care perspective, documenting continued reliance on herbal medicines alongside biomedical diabetes management ref [2]. This convergence of findings across regions supports the view that Moroccan antidiabetic ethnoflora comprises both a shared national therapeutic repertoire and localized pharmacopoeias, thereby providing a strong empirical basis for prioritizing the most culturally salient taxa for pharmacological validation and safety assessment ref [18], ref [2], ref [4], ref [5], ref [6], ref [11], ref [16], ref [17].

subsections.subsection_title: Traditional Knowledge on Diabetes Complications and Integrative Care
subsections.content:
Moroccan ethnobotanical surveys indicate that lay and specialist knowledge rarely treats diabetes as an isolated glycemic disorder; instead, it is understood through a cluster of chronic manifestations such as kidney complaints, visual decline, poor wound healing, fatigue, hypertension, and cardiovascular discomfort. In several regions, informants explicitly reported using the same or complementary plants for diabetes together with hypertension, heart disease, renal symptoms, or general inflammatory states, reflecting a practical concept of complication-oriented care rather than single-disease therapy ref [9], ref [8], ref [10], ref [6], ref [7], ref [4]. This broad therapeutic framing is also visible in North African and wider ethnopharmacological literature, where antidiabetic remedies are commonly selected for perceived benefits on circulation, urinary function, digestion, and weakness associated with long-standing disease ref [13], ref [11], ref [14].

Traditional management is therefore integrative in two senses: first, remedies are embedded in diet, lifestyle restriction, and household self-care; second, plant mixtures or sequential preparations are used to address both hyperglycemia and its downstream complications. Surveys from Morocco and comparable settings describe the co-use of medicinal plants with food regulation, reduced sugar intake, physical moderation, and symptom-based adjustment of recipes, while some preparations are reserved for neuropathic pain, skin lesions, edema, or hypertension accompanying diabetes ref [2], ref [12], ref [3], ref [1], ref [5]. Such patterns suggest that local therapeutic rationales prioritize restoring functional balance and preventing deterioration, not merely lowering blood glucose ref [19], ref [20].

For survey interpretation, this has two implications. First, reports of antidiabetic use should be read alongside emic categories of complications and comorbidities, since the indication attached to a plant may encompass vascular, renal, ocular, or digestive sequelae. Second, integrative care in Morocco likely involves dynamic combinations of phytotherapy, dietary practices, and biomedical treatment, particularly in chronic cases, underscoring the need for future fieldwork to document dosage, treatment sequencing, and perceived risk-benefit tradeoffs in complication management ref [7], ref [4], ref [12], ref [21].

subsections.subsection_title: Broader Ethnopharmacological Context of Medicinal Plant Use
subsections.content:
The Moroccan antidiabetic materia medica should be interpreted within a broader ethnopharmacological pattern observed across low- and middle-income settings, where medicinal plants are embedded in plural therapeutic systems and are used not only for glucose control but also for symptom relief, chronic inflammation, digestive complaints, and cardiovascular comorbidities. Comparative reviews from Pakistan, Sudan, Central America, and Mauritius show recurring ethnobotanical regularities: dominance of herbs, frequent use of leaves and seeds, and reliance on decoctions or infusions as the principal household preparations, indicating that Moroccan practices are part of a wider transregional logic of accessible, orally administered phytotherapy rather than an isolated repertoire ref [22], ref [2], ref [3], ref [4].

This wider context is important because many plants selected in folk medicine are valued for polyvalence rather than a single disease label. Reviews of medicinal plants used for diabetes consistently note overlap between antidiabetic use and indications related to inflammation, hypertension, obesity, liver disorders, and wound healing, suggesting that traditional selection often follows perceived whole-body benefits and management of chronic complications ref [5], ref [6]. The broader literature on inflammatory ethnomedicine in Pakistan further reinforces this point by documenting how communities repeatedly mobilize the same species across multiple chronic conditions, with Asteraceae-rich inventories, leaf-based remedies, and decoctions predominating; these patterns are useful comparators when considering why several Moroccan taxa also circulate between metabolic and inflammatory indications ref [22].

At the same time, the broader ethnopharmacological record highlights methodological and conservation issues relevant to Morocco. Cross-country reviews emphasize uneven pharmacological validation, variability in vernacular naming and preparation, and pressure on frequently harvested species, particularly where wild collection and commercial trade intersect ref [22], ref [5]. Accordingly, Moroccan survey findings should be read not only as inventories of antidiabetic remedies, but as part of a larger biocultural system in which efficacy beliefs, affordability, accessibility, and ecological sustainability jointly shape medicinal plant use ref [2], ref [3], ref [4].

This review deliberately excludes detailed genomic, metabolomic, and broad phytochemical profiling, because its primary objective is to synthesize ethnobotanical evidence on antidiabetic plant use in Morocco rather than to catalogue molecular traits of the cited taxa. Such exclusion is methodologically important: genomic resources, biosynthetic pathway studies, and chemotaxonomic surveys can illuminate evolutionary diversification and specialized metabolite production, but they do not by themselves document local therapeutic indication, preparation mode, or transmission of knowledge. A useful example is the genome of Artemisia annua, which has advanced understanding of Asteraceae evolution and terpenoid biosynthesis, yet this type of evidence lies outside the ethnobotanical scope adopted here [1].

Likewise, while many Moroccan antidiabetic plants are known from the wider literature to contain polyphenols, terpenes, alkaloids, sulfur compounds, saponins, or polysaccharides with plausible glucose-lowering, antioxidant, or anti-inflammatory activities, an exhaustive treatment of these constituents would shift the review toward phytochemistry and experimental pharmacology rather than field-based use patterns. For the same reason, we do not discuss transcriptomic regulation of secondary metabolism, marker-assisted authentication, or pathway engineering for bioactive compound production, although such approaches are increasingly relevant for medicinal plant research and valorization [1].

Accordingly, phytochemical or genomic information is mentioned only when strictly necessary to clarify taxonomic identity or to explain why a species has attracted broader pharmacological interest. This boundary helps preserve analytical coherence within the present section, which is centered on regional surveys, vernacular knowledge, therapeutic aims, and integrative care practices in Moroccan communities, while leaving molecular and compositional background to dedicated phytochemical and omics-focused reviews [1].

subsections.section_title: Traditional Antidiabetic Medicinal Plants in Moroccan Ethnopharmacology
subsections.subsection_title: Patterns of Herbal Use Among Diabetic Patients
subsections.content:
Available Moroccan surveys indicate that herbal self-care is deeply embedded in diabetes management, particularly in the eastern part of the country. In a hospital-based cross-sectional study from Oujda, 54.8% of diabetic patients reported using herbal medicines, while an earlier regional survey in Oriental Morocco found that 67.5% of patients with diabetes and/or hypertension regularly used medicinal plants, underscoring the persistence of phytotherapy across time and settings ref [24], ref [10]. These figures suggest that plant use is not marginal or occasional, but rather a routine complement to biomedical treatment among many Moroccan patients.

The profile of use is shaped by both sociodemographic and clinical factors. In Oriental Morocco, women were significantly more likely to use herbal medicines, and use was also associated with education level, menopausal status, type 2 diabetes, and combined treatment with oral antidiabetic drugs plus insulin ref [24]. Notably, patients generally did not spontaneously disclose herbal consumption to their physicians ref [24], a pattern of particular relevance given the frequent concomitant use of traditional remedies with conventional antidiabetic therapy. Such non-disclosure reflects the integrative, but often medically unsupervised, character of herbal use in Moroccan diabetes care.

Across surveys, plant selection shows both continuity and regional variation. In Oriental Morocco, the most commonly cited antidiabetic plants included Salvia officinalis, Trigonella foenum-graecum, Olea europaea, Artemisia herba-alba, and Origanum vulgare ref [24], whereas the broader northeastern survey highlighted Trigonella foenum-graecum, Globularia alypum, Artemisia herba-alba, Citrullus colocynthis, and Tetraclinis articulata ref [10]. In Beni Mellal, Olea europaea, Salvia officinalis, Allium sativum, and Trigonella foenum-graecum were among the most frequently reported species ref [18]. Taken together, these studies indicate a stable core repertoire of antidiabetic plants in Morocco, centered on a limited number of culturally validated species repeatedly mobilized by patients and traditional knowledge holders ref [24], ref [10], ref [18].

subsections.section_title: Traditional Antidiabetic Medicinal Plants in Moroccan Ethnopharmacology
subsections.subsection_title: Safety and Toxicological Considerations in Traditional Use
subsections.content:
Safety is a major concern in the traditional antidiabetic use of Moroccan medicinal plants because empirical efficacy is often transmitted without standardized dosing, duration, or contraindications. This is particularly important in diabetes, where prolonged self-medication, plant mixtures, and concurrent use with conventional hypoglycemic drugs may increase the risks of organ toxicity, herb–drug interactions, or delayed access to appropriate care. Toxicological concerns are especially relevant for species with narrow therapeutic margins or known poisonous constituents, even when they are culturally valued remedies.

Among plants reported in North African traditional medicine, some species warrant clear caution. Citrullus colocynthis has documented experimental toxicity, producing diarrhea, weight loss, hematological disturbances, and hepatorenal lesions in rats; toxicity was aggravated when combined with Nerium oleander, a highly poisonous cardiotoxic plant containing cardiac glycosides ref [25]. Peganum harmala, sometimes used for diverse folk indications including metabolic disorders, has also been associated with human intoxication, with neurological and sensory symptoms reported after ingestion ref [28]. Likewise, Ricinus communis remains a hazardous species because of ricin-related poisoning risk, making any medicinal use of seeds or poorly processed preparations potentially dangerous ref [29].

Even plants often perceived as relatively safe require qualification. Nigella sativa fixed oil showed a comparatively wide safety margin in animal studies, with no major histopathological damage after chronic oral administration, although hematological changes were noted ref [6]. By contrast, prolonged exposure to Artemisia herba-alba produced adverse reproductive effects in female rats, including reduced fertility indices after longer treatment periods ref [27]. Collectively, these data indicate that Moroccan ethnopharmacological knowledge should be interpreted alongside modern toxicology: plant identity, part used, preparation method, dose, treatment duration, and patient status (especially pregnancy, renal/hepatic disease, and polypharmacy) should all be considered before recommending traditional antidiabetic remedies ref [25], ref [27], ref [28], ref [29], ref [6].

subsections.section_title: Traditional Antidiabetic Medicinal Plants in Moroccan Ethnopharmacology
subsections.subsection_title: Regional Ethnobotanical Surveys of Antidiabetic Plants in Morocco
subsections.content:
Regional ethnobotanical surveys consistently show that antidiabetic phytotherapy is deeply embedded in Moroccan therapeutic practice, while also revealing marked geographic variation in the number of species recorded and in the taxa most frequently cited. Early large-scale surveys in Fez–Boulemane and Tafilalet documented about 90 and 92 medicinal plants, respectively, with diabetes among the main indications, underscoring the breadth of local materia medica in north-central and south-eastern Morocco ref [30], ref [9]. In Errachidia province, 45 antidiabetic species were inventoried, whereas more focused surveys identified 59 species in Sidi Slimane, 76 in the Central Middle Atlas, 40 in Izarène, and 39 in Tizi n’Test, confirming both the richness and regional specificity of diabetes-related herbal knowledge ref [8], ref [4], ref [5], ref [6], ref [8].

Despite this heterogeneity, several recurrent ethnobotanical patterns emerge across regions. Lamiaceae, Asteraceae, and Apiaceae repeatedly rank among the dominant families, and a relatively stable core of species appears in multiple surveys, notably Trigonella foenum-graecum, Olea europaea, Ajuga iva, Artemisia herba-alba, Nigella sativa, Rosmarinus officinalis, Marrubium vulgare, and Salvia spp. ref [8], ref [4], ref [6], ref [8]. Leaves and seeds are the plant parts most often employed, decoction and infusion are the prevailing preparation methods, and oral administration is overwhelmingly predominant, whether in Sidi Slimane, the Central Middle Atlas, Izarène, or Tizi n’Test ref [4], ref [5], ref [6], ref [8].

These regional surveys are not merely descriptive inventories; they also help identify locally salient candidates for pharmacological prioritization. The Meknès-Tafilalet study highlighted a smaller panel of frequently used plants such as Thymelaea hirsuta, Teucrium polium, Mentha pulegium, Artemisia absinthium, Ruta montana, and Olea europaea, linking ethnomedical selection with preliminary hypoglycemic testing ref [7]. Likewise, the Central Middle Atlas survey reported several taxa newly recorded in Moroccan antidiabetic practice, illustrating the dynamic and still incompletely documented nature of folk knowledge ref [5]. Taken together, Moroccan regional surveys provide a robust comparative framework for identifying consensus species, region-specific remedies, and research gaps relevant to standardization, efficacy assessment, and safe integration of traditional antidiabetic plants ref [30], ref [9], ref [5].

subsections.section_title: Traditional Antidiabetic Medicinal Plants in Moroccan Ethnopharmacology
subsections.subsection_title: Bioactive Antidiabetic Species and Key Phytoconstituents
subsections.content:
Among Moroccan antidiabetic plants, species with the strongest phytochemical rationale include Olea europaea, Nigella sativa, Allium cepa, and Marrubium vulgare. Olive leaves are especially notable because they are rich in phenolic secoiridoids, principally oleuropein, together with hydroxytyrosol and related biophenols that have repeatedly been associated with hypoglycemic activity ref [9], ref [10], ref [13]. In experimental diabetes, purified oleuropein lowered blood glucose, improved antioxidant status, and partially preserved pancreatic islet architecture, supporting its relevance beyond simple antioxidant supplementation ref [9].

Mechanistically, olive phenolics appear to target postprandial glucose control as well. Hydroxytyrosol and oleuropein inhibit carbohydrate-hydrolyzing enzymes, particularly α-glucosidase, with weaker effects on α-amylase, suggesting a digestive enzyme-based mechanism compatible with traditional use of olive leaf preparations ref [10]. In addition, Olea europaea contains triterpenes such as oleanolic acid and related derivatives isolated from stems, which show in vitro α-amylase inhibitory activity and broaden the antidiabetic chemical space of this culturally important Moroccan species ref [11].

Nigella sativa, another widely valued medicinal species in North African practice, contains fixed and essential oils, alkaloids, saponins, and especially thymoquinone, regarded as its principal bioactive constituent ref [35], ref [36]. Review evidence indicates glucose-lowering, lipid-improving, antioxidant, and cytoprotective actions, suggesting that its antidiabetic effects are likely multifactorial rather than attributable to a single pathway ref [35], ref [36]. Likewise, Allium cepa essential oil improved hyperglycemia, insulin status, lipid peroxidation, and tissue histology in streptozotocin-diabetic rats, implicating sulfur-containing volatile constituents in metabolic protection ref [16].

Polyphenol-rich Marrubium vulgare also deserves attention in the Maghreb context. Its infusion contains flavonoids, chlorogenic acid, and abundant verbascoside/acteoside derivatives, and produced marked antihyperglycemic and antihyperlipidemic effects in alloxan-diabetic rats ref [17]. Collectively, these data indicate that Moroccan antidiabetic ethnoflora is chemically dominated by phenolics, terpenoids, quinones, and sulfur compounds, with convergent actions on oxidative stress, pancreatic protection, lipid metabolism, and intestinal carbohydrate digestion ref [35], ref [10], ref [13], ref [17].

subsections.section_title: Traditional Antidiabetic Medicinal Plants in Moroccan Ethnopharmacology
subsections.subsection_title: Preclinical Validation of Commonly Used Moroccan Antidiabetic Plants
subsections.content:
Preclinical studies provide important support for several antidiabetic plants repeatedly reported in Moroccan ethnopharmacology. In streptozotocin (STZ)-diabetic rat models, aqueous extracts of Ammodaucus leucotrichus fruits, Eucalyptus globulus leaves, Rubus fructicosus leaves, and Globularia alypum leaves all produced significant reductions in blood glucose, thereby lending experimental credibility to their traditional use in Morocco ref [39], ref [41], ref [43]. Notably, A. leucotrichus also improved oral glucose tolerance, showed antioxidant activity in vitro, and attenuated diabetes-associated liver histological damage, suggesting effects beyond simple glycemic lowering ref [39].

Other widely used Mediterranean/Moroccan taxa have also shown preclinical efficacy. Ficus carica leaf decoction lowered plasma glucose in STZ-diabetic rats without stimulating insulin secretion, pointing to a likely peripheral or extra-pancreatic mechanism ref [40]. Similarly, aqueous preparations of G. alypum and R. fructicosus reduced glycemia in diabetic animals without significant changes in insulin output, again suggesting non-secretagogue actions ref [43]. For E. globulus, antihyperglycemic activity was demonstrated in both normal and diabetic rats, reinforcing the pharmacological relevance of a species frequently cited in Moroccan herbal practice ref [41].

Validation has also expanded to species with broader metabolic effects. Olea europaea leaf extracts decreased serum glucose and improved insulin and lipid-related parameters in diabetic rats, with additional evidence of organ-protective effects in later STZ studies ref [46], ref [10]. Marrubium vulgare methanolic extract ameliorated hyperglycemia, dyslipidemia, oxidative stress, and tissue glycogen depletion in diabetic rats ref [12]. Although Myrtus communis is less consistently highlighted in Moroccan diabetes surveys, experimental work on different leaf extracts showed moderate glucose-lowering activity and possible synergy with glibenclamide, illustrating how extraction method can strongly influence efficacy ref [42]. Collectively, these animal data substantiate Moroccan traditional knowledge, while also underscoring persistent gaps in standardization, dose translation, and mechanistic validation before clinical extrapolation.

Overall, the Moroccan literature indicates a rich and persistent ethnopharmacological repertoire for diabetes management, documented across diverse regions including the Middle Atlas, Tafilalet, Sidi Slimane, Errachidia, Oriental Morocco, Izarène, Meknès-Tafilalet, Taroudant, and Beni Mellal, with recurrent use of taxa such as Olea europaea, Nigella sativa, Trigonella foenum-graecum, Artemisia herba-alba, and Marrubium vulgare [1–10]. This consistency across geographically distinct surveys strengthens the cultural validity of the reported practices, while also highlighting the central role of traditional knowledge in self-care among Moroccan patients with diabetes [11].

However, the evidence base remains uneven. Although several Moroccan or regionally relevant plants have shown promising hypoglycemic, antihyperlipidemic, antioxidant, or enzyme-inhibitory effects in experimental models, translation to clinical use is still limited by insufficient botanical standardization, incomplete phytochemical characterization, inadequate dose harmonization, and the scarcity of controlled human studies [12–16]. Safety is another major concern, especially for plants associated with intrinsic toxicity or poisoning risk, such as Peganum harmala, Citrullus colocynthis, Ricinus communis, and some Artemisia species, underscoring that traditional use does not guarantee safety [17–20].

Future work should therefore move from descriptive inventories toward integrated validation pipelines: rigorous voucher-based identification, reproducible extract standardization, mechanistic studies targeting insulin signaling, carbohydrate-digesting enzymes and oxidative stress, followed by well-designed clinical trials and pharmacovigilance [13,15,16,21]. Equally important are studies on herb–drug interactions, real-world usage patterns, and conservation of frequently harvested species, so that Moroccan antidiabetic ethnoflora can be translated into safe, evidence-based, and culturally grounded complementary therapies [11,14,22].
